note.specFocus: Christian beliefs about death, resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, contrasted with non-religious views.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
2.1 Death and Life After Death
Christian belief about death centres on the resurrection of Jesus, which is treated as both proof and guarantee of life beyond physical death for believers.
Resurrection and judgement
• 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Jesus "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep", meaning his resurrection is the first example of a resurrection all believers hope to share.
• Most Christians believe in a final judgement, at which each person's life is assessed by God, leading to eternal life in heaven (full relationship with God) or separation from God, often called hell.
• Catholic teaching additionally includes purgatory, a state of purification after death for those who die in God's friendship but are not yet fully ready for heaven; most Protestants reject purgatory, emphasising judgement and salvation through faith at the point of death.
Why believe in life after death?
• John 3:16 promises that "whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life" — a central motivation for Christian hope.
• Belief in ultimate justice: if good people suffer unfairly and wrongdoers sometimes prosper in this life, an afterlife allows for final justice.
Non-religious views
• Humanists argue personality and consciousness depend entirely on the brain, so death is the permanent end of a person's existence; this life is the only one we have, giving strong reason to make it meaningful now.
Exam link: distinguish clearly between "non-religious reasons to believe in an afterlife" (e.g. near-death experiences) and "non-religious reasons to reject an afterlife" (e.g. no evidence of consciousness without a brain) — questions can ask for either.

questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, Christians believe that Jesus' own resurrection from the dead, described in all four Gospels, is the foundation and guarantee of life after death for believers; 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Jesus "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep".

Second, Most Christians believe in a final judgement after death, at which God will judge each person's life, leading to eternal life in heaven with God or separation from God, often called hell.

Finally, Catholic Christians additionally believe in purgatory, a state of purification for those who die in God's friendship but are not yet fully ready for heaven, while most Protestant Christians reject purgatory and emphasise judgement and salvation through faith alone at the point of death.
questions.question: Choose one religion. Explain what its followers believe about life after death.

questions.examTip: For a 12-mark evaluation, use accurate religious teaching, explain different religious or non-religious views, analyse the statement and reach a justified conclusion. The conclusion should follow from the arguments you have discussed.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Humanists and other non-religious people argue that there is no scientific evidence of consciousness surviving death; personality and memory appear to depend entirely on a functioning brain, which suggests death is simply the end of a person's existence.

A second consideration is: If this life is the only one we have, some argue it gives people a strong motive to focus on making this world better and more just, rather than relying on a future life to put things right.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Christians point to the resurrection of Jesus as historical testimony, recorded by multiple witnesses in the Gospels, that death is not the end; this event is treated as the basis for the promise in John 3:16 that "whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life".

A further consideration is: Christians also argue that a loving, just God would not allow the apparent injustices of this life, where good people often suffer and wrongdoers sometimes prosper, to be the final word; life after death is needed for ultimate justice.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: this debate often comes down to whether someone trusts the testimony behind religious claims such as the resurrection, or requires independent, empirical evidence before accepting that anything continues beyond physical death. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of resurrection, judgement, heaven, hell and different Christian interpretations of the afterlife and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
